about:
I'm currently a junior at Wentworth Institute of Technology pursuing a Bachelor of Science in Mechanical Engineering with a minor in Aerospace Engineering. I have hands on experience in engineering design and real world project environments, with a strong interest in building practical, high impact solutions.

Through my co-op roles, I've contributed to large-scale engineering projects ranging from mission-critical data centers to complex building systems. My coursework has helped me build a strong technical foundation, which I've applied through personal and academic work focused on hands on design and problem-solving. I've developed experience across multiple CAD and BIM platforms, giving me a versatile design skill set and the ability to adapt quickly in different engineering environments.

Outside of work, I enjoy taking on hands on engineering challenges, from prototype development to working on projects on my car that allow me to learn a new skill. I'm especially interested in opportunities that combine design, manufacturing, and problem solving, and I'm always looking to keep improving as an engineer.
vanderweil: At Vanderweil Engineers, I worked as a Fire Protection Engineer Co-op, independently developing fire alarm and sprinkler system layouts in Revit and producing BIM models and construction drawings. I applied NFPA and IBC codes across projects, including luxury high-rises, mission-critical data centers, and more, while collaborating with other engineering teams to resolve clashes and ensure coordinated, code-compliant designs.
integra: At Integra Mission Critical, I worked as a Project Engineer Co-op supporting the delivery of a 235,000 sq. ft. 48 MW data center. I managed RFIs and submittals, led coordination meetings with engineering and architectural teams to resolve technical issues, and conducted site visits to verify construction progress. I also performed installation and QA/QC checks on critical systems, including diesel generators, chillers, and PMDCs, helping to identify issues and support a smooth turnover process.
mazda:
I took on the challenge of rebuilding this previously totaled 2008 Mazda 3, which had suffered severe damage to the front end. As a result of the crash, the engine initially did not start, and the vehicle exhibited multiple system level issues, including overheating and lean air/fuel operating conditions after getting it to turn over.

To address this, I first conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the engine bay, chassis, and front end structural components to identify the root causes of failure. This involved diagnosing mechanical damage, tracing vacuum and cooling system faults, and assessing which components required replacement versus repair. The objective was to restore the vehicle to a safe, fully functional operating condition through a complete front end reconstruction.

I began by stripping all damaged front-end components, including the hood, bumper, fenders, headlights, radiator support, and crash bar, to fully expose the engine bay and assess system damage.

This teardown revealed a severely damaged, leaking radiator causing overheating, along with broken and deformed vacuum lines in the intake manifold that led to an improper air-fuel ratio and rough idle. This step was critical in identifying root causes and defining a clear rebuild plan.

As purchasing individual replacement parts would have been too expensive, I sourced a donor vehicle from Facebook Marketplace. While most of the body panels and cooling system components were straightforward swaps, I encountered a major challenge when addressing the vacuum line system. The donor vehicle had a different engine configuration, and the intake manifold design did not include the required vacuum ports.

To resolve this, I engineered a bypass solution directly on the intake manifold. The original issue stemmed from two 1/8 inch inner diameter vacuum nipples that had sheared off. Due to the location and severity of the damage, a reliable repair was not feasible. Instead, I evaluated the system requirements and determined that the exact physical location of the vacuum ports was not critical, as long as the correct diameter and function were maintained.

Based on this, I created two new vacuum connection points by precision tapping into the intake manifold and installing custom brass fittings. To ensure a secure and leak free seal under high engine temperatures, I additionally reinforced the fittings with a high heat resistant liquid epoxy. I also replaced the vacuum lines with new tubing matched to the required inner diameter for proper fitment and performance. Finally, I sealed the original failed ports using a putty style epoxy to prevent any air leakage and restore system integrity.

Following the repair and reassembly process, I conducted thorough testing and troubleshooting to verify system performance across all major functions. This included confirming stable engine startup, resolving overheating issues, and restoring proper air/fuel operation with a smooth idle. The project ultimately returned the vehicle to a safe, fully operable condition, and it has since been successfully driven on the road for over four months with no issues.

This project reinforced my ability to diagnose complex system failures, adapt designs under constraints, and execute hands on engineering solutions from teardown through final validation.
gearbox: As part of a three person team, I contributed to the engineering design of a single stage spur gearbox required to transmit 4 horsepower at 2000 rpm under light shock loading while achieving a target gear ratio of 4.5:1 (±2%). The objective was to develop a fully functional, manufacturable gearbox that satisfied performance, reliability, and safety constraints, including fatigue life, bearing longevity, and proper function between components. I primarily used Autodesk Inventor and SolidWorks for the design.

I began with a system level design approach, breaking the gearbox into its core parts: gears, shafts, bearings, and housing. Before moving into detailed calculations, I first developed a preliminary hand sketch of the gearbox to visualize how all components would integrate. This rough concept helped map the overall structure of the gears, shaft alignment, and power flow through the system, ensuring that the design was feasible.

Gear geometry was then developed through detailed analytical calculations, including diametral pitch, tooth count, pitch diameters, and contact ratio. A final gear set of 21 teeth (for the pinion) and 95 teeth (for the gear) achieved a ratio of 4.52:1, remaining well within the required tolerance. Loading analysis was then performed to determine transmitted forces, torque, and resulting stresses across the system.

The design focused on ensuring the structural integrity of the gearbox under operating conditions. AGMA based bending and contact stress analyses were conducted to verify that stresses remained below allowable material limits while maintaining appropriate factors of safety. Shaft design was also carried out using combined loading and fatigue criteria, accounting for stress concentrations from features such as fillets, keyways, and retaining ring grooves.

Final shaft dimensions of 1 inch for the input shaft and 2 inches for the output shaft were selected to provide conservative strength margins and minimize deflection.

To account for real world operating conditions, the design incorporated an overload factor of 1.5, resulting in a delivered design power of 6 horsepower. This ensured the gearbox was evaluated under worst case loading conditions rather than nominal operating power. All force, torque, and stress calculations were based on this adjusted power input to improve system reliability and safety under loads.

Bearing selection and sizing were carried out through reaction force calculations at each support to determine the radial and axial loads acting on the system. These reaction forces were then used to evaluate both the static and dynamic load requirements of the bearings. The design criteria specified a 97.5% reliability target and a required service life of 4,000 hours, which were incorporated into the life equations to determine the minimum acceptable dynamic load rating. Based on these calculations and constraints, we decided to go with SKF as the manufacturer, and we selected Deep Groove Ball Bearings (Part# 6204-2RSJEM) for the input and output shafts. These bearings provided adequate capacity to support combined loading while maintaining the required reliability and operational lifespan.

Key design and verification were carried out using Autodesk Inventor to ensure proper fit and load transfer between the gear and shaft. The selected configuration was a square key for the gear/shaft connection. This size was chosen based on the transmitted torque, shaft diameter, and standard key design guidelines to prevent failure in shear and bearing. The analysis confirmed that the key provides sufficient capacity to safely transmit the required loads without excessive stress concentration, while maintaining manufacturability and proper alignment between the gear and shaft assembly.

Lubrication was also specified to ensure efficient operation and reduce wear at the gear mesh. An ISO VG 150 gear oil (Mobilgear 600 XP 150) was selected based on its viscosity grade and suitability for moderate speed, moderate load gear systems. This lubricant provides an effective film thickness for reducing friction, minimizing surface fatigue, and improving overall gearbox reliability and service life.

We successfully designed a manufacturable gearbox that meets all required specifications. Safety factors for gear stresses, shaft fatigue, and bearing life were all verified. Overall, the project demonstrates a practical application of machine design principles in developing a reliable, accurate, and production ready mechanical system, resulting in a reliable and manufacturable final design.
rotor: For this project, I conducted a transient thermal analysis of a brake rotor under a 3 second, 60 - 0 mph short duration braking event representing a ~3,100 lb passenger vehicle. The goal was to understand how heat builds up in the rotor over a rapid braking interval and how design changes affect thermal performance.

The first step was to model the brake rotor in SOLIDWORKS. I researched typical brake rotor designs and used them as a reference for my model. I then set up a transient thermal simulation to capture temperature changes over time. The simulation was run over a 3 second braking interval using 0.1 second time steps to accurately represent the rapid heat buildup. I selected gray cast iron to be the applied material, as this is typically used in automotive rotors.

After running an initial baseline simulation, I analyzed the temperature distribution and identified areas of high thermal concentration. I then optimized the design by modifying key geometric features of the rotor. This included adding drilled holes to enhance heat dissipation, as well as adjusting the size and configuration of the internal vanes to improve airflow and internal heat distribution. After each design modification, I re-ran the transient thermal simulation to compare results and evaluate performance improvements.

The thermal loading in the simulation represented a short, high energy braking event in which the vehicle's kinetic energy is converted into heat at the rotor over a brief period. To model this, I conducted background research of typical conditions and applied three primary thermal conditions: a heat power input of approximately 18,000 W to represent braking energy from a ~3,100 lb vehicle, a convective heat transfer coefficient of 90 W/m²·K to simulate cooling from airflow over the rotor, and an ambient/initial temperature of 77°F (25°C), assuming the rotor started at a uniform temperature. Together, these conditions allowed the simulation to capture both rapid heat generation and convective cooling, providing a realistic representation of rotor behavior during braking.

The optimized rotor design reached peak temperatures of approximately 395°F during the 3-second braking simulation, which represented a deceleration from 60 mph to 0 mph. Compared to the initial design, the improved geometry produced a more uniform temperature distribution and reduced localized hot spots. The addition of drilled holes and refined internal vane geometry enhanced heat dissipation by decreasing surface area and improving airflow through the rotor.

Overall, this project demonstrated my ability to apply heat transfer principles to a real world mechanical system and use simulation driven design to improve performance. By optimizing the design and analyzing transient thermal behavior, I was able to develop a more thermally efficient rotor design while strengthening my skills in CAD modeling, engineering analysis, and data driven optimization.
